summary: Source-anchored research for Atlas IP access lists. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Pending means Atlas is configuring an entry; Active means configuration covers every provisioned project container. Active in regions is specific to AWS security groups. (low confidence)
Adding any IPv4 /0 CIDR entry, including 0.0.0.0/0 or 10.0.0.0/0, causes Atlas to send an alert email to users granted a project role directly or through a team with a project role. (low confidence)

In its SRV connection-string troubleshooting procedure, MongoDB directs checking both the application server IP in the Atlas IP access list and outbound TCP port 27017 through the firewall when the end-to-end network test fails. (low confidence)

MongoDB’s IP access-list page applies to Atlas Core and Atlas Infinite. An entry represents a single IP address or a CIDR-notated range; the page also describes AWS security-group entries associated with a same-region peered VPC. The project IP access list applies to every cluster in that project. MongoDB documents a limit of 200 entries, except projects with an existing sharded cluster created before August 25, 2017, whose limit is 100 entries. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
A standard project IP access list cannot restrict access to the Atlas UI. MongoDB directs customers to the organization UI IP Access List for that purpose. (low confidence)
Temporary entries expire within a configurable 7-day period. The UI offers 6 hours, 1 day, or 1 week; AWS security groups cannot be temporary entries. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
A temporary entry can have its duration changed or become permanent. A permanent entry cannot be changed to temporary. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

In its SRV connection-string troubleshooting procedure, MongoDB identifies driver version as another possible cause when all listed network tests pass but the error persists; it describes updating the driver or using the standard non-SRV connection string. (low confidence)
Microsoft’s Atlas discovery guide says a TLS handshake error indicates failure at the transport layer and does not by itself prove an incorrect database username or password. (low confidence)
A failed ping test can reflect blocked ICMP rather than a TCP connection problem; MongoDB directs proceeding to the end-to-end network connection test. (low confidence)
Managing entries requires Project Owner or Project Network Access Manager access. Organization Owners must add themselves to the project as Project Owner. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)
The project Activity Feed records access-list creation, deletion, and changes. Changing an address produces deletion and creation activities, but comment updates are not reported. (low confidence)

An AWS security-group entry grants access through membership in a peered VPC. MongoDB does not support these entries in projects with VPC peering connections in multiple regions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Deleting an access-list entry may leave existing connections from the removed addresses open for a variable time, depending on connection establishment, application or driver behavior, and protocol. (low confidence)
If home or office access stops unexpectedly, Atlas recommends checking whether the current public IP still matches an entry. (low confidence)

Microsoft distinguishes Atlas Admin API discovery restrictions attached to the API credential from database connection restrictions controlled by the project IP access list and cluster private networking. (low confidence)
The generated Atlas CLI project IP access-list API commands support creating, deleting, retrieving, listing, and checking entry status. (low confidence)

In the November 2025 issue, a reporter using AKO 2.11.0 described competing `AtlasIPAccessList` resources overwriting entries; maintainers said the operator expected one list resource per project and treated it as sole owner. (low confidence)
The AWS and MongoDB coauthored April 2026 article says organization-level Atlas Resource Policies can prevent wildcard IP access in access lists. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-04-23)

For a cluster that remains unreachable after its source IP is allowed, troubleshoot endpoint reachability, firewall, DNS, and TLS settings as well. MongoDB and Microsoft both document additional network checks beyond the project IP access list. (medium confidence)

MongoDB warns that a /0 CIDR permits access from anywhere and can expose the deployment to unauthorized access and data exfiltration. It recommends trusted IP addresses or CIDR ranges and strong database-user credentials for public Internet access. (low confidence)

Private endpoints can coexist with other Atlas access methods, including public IP access-list entries and network peering. Clients connecting through those other methods use standard connection strings. (low confidence)

For SRV connection troubleshooting, MongoDB directs testing the DNS SRV record, each node hostname, ping and end-to-end network connectivity from the application server experiencing the issue. (low confidence)

The cited SRV troubleshooting procedure uses port 27017 in its fixed-port firewall check, while its host discovery and end-to-end test use the selected connection method’s node hostnames and port numbers. For an AWS PrivateLink access path, MongoDB documents Atlas-assigned ports 1024 through 65535 that can change, recommends the DNS seedlist private endpoint-aware connection string and allowing the entire range, and shows SRV answers containing distinct assigned ports. Apply the host-and-port test to that endpoint-aware SRV target and port for an AWS PrivateLink route; a fixed test on port 27017 alone does not check those other assigned endpoint ports. (medium confidence)

The current AtlasIPAccessList reference states that each project supports at most one AtlasIPAccessList resource and that multiple resources for the same project conflict. It describes the operator creating a new project IP access list or replacing an existing list. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-11)
The current AtlasIPAccessList reference states that Atlas Kubernetes Operator does not support Atlas Infinite Database clusters in public preview. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-11)

The operator reference states that, as of Atlas Kubernetes Operator 2.0, deleting a custom resource in Kubernetes does not by default delete the corresponding object in Atlas; the operator instead stops managing that Atlas resource. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-11)
